patterns.name: SVO basic word order
patterns.explanation: Chinese declarative sentences follow a strict Subject-Verb-Object order, just like English. Nouns carry no case marking and verbs never conjugate, so word order — not inflection — is the primary signal of who does what to whom. Keep the subject before the verb and the object after it; time and place phrases go before the verb.

patterns.name: No inflection — context/time words carry tense
patterns.explanation: Chinese verbs have no tense, number, or gender inflection: 吃 (chī) can mean eat, eats, ate, or eating depending on context. Tense is understood from time words (昨天 yesterday, 明天 tomorrow), surrounding context, or aspect particles such as 了. The verb form never changes.

patterns.name: Topic-comment
patterns.explanation: Chinese is topic-prominent: a sentence often starts with the topic — what the sentence is about, frequently the object — followed by a comment about it. The topic is usually old or known information, and the comment (subject + predicate) supplies the new information. This lets speakers put known information first.

examples.pinyin: zhè běn shū wǒ kàn guò

examples.english: Chinese is hard. (As for Chinese, it is difficult.)

patterns.name: Time placement
patterns.explanation: Time words come before the verb — usually at the very start of the sentence (before the subject) or right after the subject. Unlike English, they never appear at the end after the object.

examples.english: I am going to school today.
We drink coffee in the morning.

patterns.name: 吗 (ma) yes/no questions
patterns.explanation: To turn a statement into a yes/no question, simply add the particle 吗 (ma) at the end. The word order stays exactly the same — there is no auxiliary verb and no inversion.

examples.english: Are you eating? / Do you want to eat?

examples.pinyin: zhè shì nǐ de shū ma

patterns.name: A-not-A (V不V) questions
patterns.explanation: Yes/no questions can also be formed with the A-not-A pattern: state the verb, then 不 (bù), then the verb again — 你吃不吃? 'Are you eating (or not)?' This is direct and common in everyday speech. 是 (to be) and 有 (to have) use 是不是 / 有没有.

patterns.name: Measure words (个 general + noun-specific)
patterns.explanation: Chinese nouns must be counted with a measure word (classifier) placed between the number and the noun. 个 (gè) is the general measure word for people and many everyday objects; specific nouns take specific measure words, such as 本 (běn) for books and 张 (zhāng) for flat objects like paper and tables.

patterns.name: Serial verb constructions
patterns.explanation: Chinese allows two or more verbs to appear one after another in a single sentence, sharing the same subject, with no conjunction in between. Common uses are go-and-do and come-and-do patterns, such as 我去买东西 ('I go buy things').

examples.english: I am going to buy things.
I go to school to study.

patterns.name: Pro-drop (omitted subject)
patterns.explanation: When the subject is clear from context, Chinese often omits it entirely — especially pronouns such as I, you, and he. This is called pro-drop. English requires an explicit subject in every clause; Chinese leaves it out when the listener can infer it.

patterns.name: 了 (le) perfective aspect
patterns.explanation: The aspect particle 了 (le) marks a completed action or a change of state — something that has already happened. Chinese has no past-tense conjugation; 了 placed after the verb signals completion.

patterns.name: 着 (zhe) durative aspect
patterns.explanation: The particle 着 (zhe) marks an ongoing or continuous state — an action or state that is in progress or holding. It often describes a static posture or an activity continuing in the background, as in 他吃着饭 ('he is in the middle of eating').

examples.english: He is eating (in the middle of a meal).

patterns.name: 过 (guò) experiential aspect
patterns.explanation: The particle 过 (guò) marks an experience — something that has happened at least once in the past ('have ever done'). Use it when asking or stating whether someone has experienced an action.

examples.english: Have you ever been to Beijing?

patterns.name: 正在 (zhèngzài) progressive aspect
patterns.explanation: The adverb 正在 (zhèngzài) marks an action in progress right now — equivalent to the English '-ing' / 'am/is/are doing'. It comes before the verb; 在 or 正 alone can carry the same progressive meaning.

patterns.name: 的 (de) possessive / modifier
patterns.explanation: The particle 的 (de) links a modifier to a noun: possession (我的书 'my book'), description, or relationship. It marks that the first element modifies the second. Pronoun + 的 + noun is the standard way to say 'my / your / his...'.

patterns.name: 地 (de) adverb marker
patterns.explanation: The particle 地 (de) turns an adjective or descriptive phrase into an adverb that modifies a verb — 慢慢地走 means 'walk slowly'. 地 sits between the adverbial phrase and the verb. (Written 地 but pronounced the same as 的 and 得.)

patterns.name: 得 (de) resultative complement
patterns.explanation: The particle 得 (de) links a verb to a complement describing how well or to what degree the action is done — 做得很好 means 'done very well'. It is used to evaluate performance or describe the result of an action.

patterns.name: 因为...所以 cause-consequence
patterns.explanation: 因为 (yīnwèi, 'because') introduces the reason and 所以 (suǒyǐ, 'so / therefore') introduces the result. Both halves usually appear together: 因为我累，所以不去 — 'Because I am tired, (so) I am not going.'

examples.pinyin: yīnwèi wǒ lèi, suǒyǐ bù qù
examples.english: Because I am tired, I am not going.

examples.chinese: 因为天气不好，所以我们不去。
examples.pinyin: yīnwèi tiānqì bù hǎo, suǒyǐ wǒmen bù qù
examples.english: Because the weather is bad, we are not going.

examples.chinese: 因为他喜欢中文，所以他学习。
examples.pinyin: yīnwèi tā xǐhuan zhōngwén, suǒyǐ tā xuéxí
examples.english: Because he likes Chinese, he studies it.

patterns.name: 把 (bǎ) disposal construction
patterns.explanation: The 把 (bǎ) construction moves the object before the verb and marks it as the thing being disposed of or affected, emphasizing the result of the action on the object: 我把书放在桌子上 — 'I put the book on the table.' Use it when the verb is followed by a complement describing what happens to the object.

examples.pinyin: wǒ bǎ shū fàng zài zhuōzi shàng
examples.english: I put the book on the table.
I give the money to him.

patterns.name: 被 (bèi) passive construction
patterns.explanation: The 被 (bèi) construction forms the passive: the subject is the receiver of the action, and 被 introduces the agent, which may be omitted. 他被打了 — 'He was hit.' It is especially common for negative or unfortunate events.

examples.english: The apple was eaten by me.

patterns.name: 比 (bǐ) comparison
patterns.explanation: The 比 (bǐ) construction expresses comparison: 'A 比 B + adjective' means 'A is more adjective than B'. The adjective follows both items; there is no separate comparative word like English '-er / more'. Add 更 (gèng, 'even more') for degree.

patterns.name: 是...的 (shì...de) emphasis construction
patterns.explanation: The 是...的 construction emphasizes a specific detail about a past event — often when, where, or how something happened: 我是昨天来的 — 'It was yesterday that I came.' The emphasized word goes between 是 and 的.

examples.english: It was yesterday that I came.

examples.pinyin: tā shì zuò dìtiě lái de
zhè běn shū shì wǒ mǎi de
examples.english: It was me who bought this book.

metadata.note: Both form yes/no questions — 吗 particle vs A-not-A (V不V).
了 perfective (completed) vs 着 durative (ongoing) — the two most-confused aspect particles.
了 marks completion of a specific action; 过 marks experience ('have ever done').
了 = completed; 正在 = in progress right now.
着 and 正在 both express continuous / progressive aspect.
的 and 地 are the same written-de family: possessive/modifier vs adverb marker.
的 (modifier) and 得 (resultative complement) share the de pronunciation.
地 marks adverbs before verbs; 得 links a verb to a result/degree complement.
The 把 construction is built on topic-prominence — understand topic-comment first.
把-sentences commonly complete with 了 (他把衣服洗了) — know 了 before 把.
把 = disposal (agent acts on object); 被 = passive (subject receives the action). The advanced-tier pair.
比 (comparison) and 是...的 (emphasis) — the supplementary advanced-HSK-tier patterns.
